definition: To teach someone in a way that improves their mind or character.
example: The professor's short essays on friendship edify readers without ever sounding preachy.
nuance: Inform means passing on facts, while edify means improving someone morally or intellectually. It has nothing to do with building an edifice.
prompt: A history museum is planning a new exhibit on early farming villages.
options: The curators designed the exhibit to edify visitors, not merely to entertain them.
Workers will edify a new glass wing on the museum's east side next spring.
The sloppy, mislabeled displays edified visitors by leaving them more confused than before.
A volunteer edified the sign by fixing two spelling errors in its first line.
reasons: Wanting visitors to leave wiser, not just amused, fits the idea of improving the mind.
This mixes the verb up with edifice. Putting up a building does nothing to improve anyone's mind.
Leaving people more muddled is the reverse of improving their understanding.
Correcting a text is editing. The verb applies to people's minds, not to signs.

practice.prompt: A soccer coach speaks to her team after a hard loss.
options: She edified the players by mocking each of their errors in front of the crowd.
The coach edified the players that the bus would leave at six o'clock sharp.
The scoreboard edified the final score in bright red numbers above the field.
Her quiet talk on learning from mistakes seemed to edify the whole team.
reasons: Public ridicule humiliates people instead of lifting them up, so nothing is improved.
Announcing a departure time only passes on a fact. It does not deepen anyone's mind or character.
A scoreboard only displays numbers. It takes a lesson or an example to improve a person.
The talk gave the players lasting insight, which is the kind of growth the verb describes.
